CT4100 Overview Web search Retrieval models

CT4100 Topic Guide

Learning to rank

Learn a ranking function from examples instead of fixing every weight by hand.

Exam-use protocol

Before writing, identify the command word: calculate/trace requires an ordered derivation; explain requires a definition, mechanism and assumption; compare/design requires matched criteria, a justified choice and a limitation. The topic-specific recall and worked routes below are the material to adapt—not text to copy blindly.

Part-by-part recall: definitions, assumptions and mechanics

Definitions: LTR learns score(q,d) from judged examples; pointwise predicts grades, pairwise preferences and listwise an ordering. Click labels are position-biased. Compare: hand-tuned ranking is interpretable; neural LTR learns representations but costs data/compute and transparency. Question cue: name examples, features, loss, held-out queries and ranking metric.

Worked practice 1 — paper-style synthesis (recurring-topic pattern; not a quoted paper prompt) LTR

Question demand: dA grade 3, dB grade 1 for q: make a pairwise example. Plan/choice: form preference, not a class. Worked answer: impose score(q,dA)>score(q,dB) using BM25/title/freshness features; tune on held-out queries by NDCG/MAP. Mark-winning points: query grouping and ranking metric. Common trap: classification accuracy.

Worked practice 2 — paper-style synthesis (recurring-topic pattern; not a quoted paper prompt) neural comparison

Question demand: Compare neural/traditional LTR for jobs. Plan/choice: organise representation, compute, interpretability and safeguards. Worked answer: traditional LTR uses engineered fast/explainable features; neural learns semantic text but raises data, GPU/latency and audit needs. Debias labels and check held-out NDCG/fairness. Mark-winning points: operational consequence per contrast. Common trap: neural automatically better/unbiased.

Purpose and module relevance

Learning mechanisms in IR are an official CT4100 outcome. Learning to Rank (LTR) combines many signals, such as text match, freshness and link features, to order documents.

What a question is really asking

Describe the training signal, feature representation, learning objective and ranking evaluation. Plan: construct query-document examples; define relevance labels/click caveats; choose pointwise, pairwise or listwise learning; evaluate with ranking metrics.

Prerequisites, vocabulary and notation

  • Feature vector x(q,d): measurable query-document signals.
  • Pointwise: predict a relevance grade; pairwise: prefer d+ over d−; listwise: optimise the ordered list.
  • Training/validation/test split: prevents overclaiming from memorised examples.
  • Neural LTR: learned representations/scorers, often less interpretable.

Method: build an LTR pipeline

  1. Collect judged query-document pairs or carefully debiased interaction data.
  2. Create features: BM25, title match, document quality, freshness and link signals.
  3. Choose a target: grade, preferred pair, or ranked-list objective.
  4. Train on past queries and tune only on validation queries.
  5. Evaluate on held-out queries with MAP/NDCG and inspect fairness, latency and feature leakage.

Worked practice 3 — foundational calculation

Question

For one query, dA is labelled 3 and dB is labelled 1. What pairwise training preference is created?

Model answer

Create the constraint score(q,dA)>score(q,dB). A pairwise loss penalises the model if it reverses them. It learns an ordering, not necessarily that “3” is a universally calibrated score.

Question interpretation and independent practice

Build confidence

Why can raw clicks be biased labels? Check: high-ranked results get seen more, so clicks partly reflect position, not relevance.

Exam bridge

Propose LTR for job search. Outline: labels and debiasing; features; pairwise/listwise choice; held-out NDCG; explanation, fairness and latency concerns.

High-value traps and corrections

Paper basis for the integrated practice: local 2025/26 learning-to-rank material was verified; this feature, bias and evaluation scenario is newly written rather than a paper adaptation.

Integrated paper-style practice - train a ranker [9 marks]

Scenario. For “late library opening”, D1 is highly relevant, D2 partly relevant, D3 irrelevant. Features are BM25, title match, opening-hours freshness and historical clicks. Propose a training signal and an evaluation that does not treat clicks as ground truth.

Question-demand diagnosis: give labels, features, an objective and defensible validation.

Fastest route: form D1>D2, D1>D3 and D2>D3 preference pairs, then test on held-out queries.

Worked answer: A pairwise learner raises preferred-document scores using lexical, title and freshness features. Clicks may be a feature only after position-bias correction, as top results are seen more. Split by query and time to avoid leakage. Evaluate nDCG@k against held-out editorial judgments, then check a guarded online test for abandonment and reformulation. A model that learns stale popularity instead of current opening times must be retrained or constrained.

Topic-specific trap: random document-level splits leak the same query into training and test.

  • Training and testing on the same queries.
  • Calling clicks ground truth.
  • Using classification accuracy instead of a ranking-aware measure.

Final answer checklist

  • Are examples, features and objective distinguished?
  • Have I named a held-out ranking metric?
  • Did I cover bias or interpretability?

Past-paper pattern

Learning to Rank and learned weights appear in 2024/25 and 2025/26 material. Neural LTR is lower-confidence/intermittent: understand its trade-offs, but do not assume a dedicated question.
